shots.narration: Rome, the fifteenth of March, 44 BC. The most powerful man in the world walks into a meeting of the Senate.
shots.onScreen: Caesar in a purple-bordered toga walks up marble steps into the Curia of Pompey, morning light
shots.motion: low angle tracking behind him up the steps

shots.narration: His name is Gaius Julius Caesar. Dictator for life.
shots.onScreen: Caesar's face, calm brows, laurel wreath; name callout
shots.overlay: callout: GAIUS JULIUS CAESAR / DICTATOR FOR LIFE

shots.narration: Outside the door, a group of gladiators waits in the courtyard, trying not to be noticed.
shots.onScreen: Gladiators loitering among columns, helmets under arms

shots.narration: His closest ally, Mark Antony, should be at his side. But someone has stopped him at the door to talk.
shots.onScreen: Antony held in conversation outside by another senator, looking away from the door

shots.narration: Caesar takes his seat on a golden chair at the front of the room. He is alone.
shots.onScreen: The golden chair, Caesar sits; the doors behind close

shots.narration: Across the room, one senator stands up and starts walking toward him.
shots.onScreen: A senator rises from the benches; dozens of eyes follow

shots.narration: In the next few minutes, more than sixty men will try to save the Roman Republic. And in doing it, they will destroy it.
shots.onScreen: Ring of togas closing around the chair, seen from above

shots.narration: This is the most famous killing in history.
shots.onScreen: "THE IDES OF MARCH" title slams over the Senate hall, laurel emblem

shots.narration: To understand how Caesar got here, we have to go back.
shots.onScreen: The golden chair fades to a young Caesar in a plain toga

shots.narration: Over almost forty years in politics, Caesar climbed to Rome's highest office. Consul.
shots.onScreen: Caesar climbing a staircase of office titles, "CONSUL" at the top

shots.narration: As a general, he conquered all of Gaul. Today that is France, Belgium and parts of Switzerland, Germany and the Netherlands.
shots.onScreen: Parchment map; Gaul floods Roman red, modern names in small labels
shots.motion: crane over Gaul as it fills

shots.narration: He was a military genius, and charming with it. His legions were loyal to him, and only him.
shots.onScreen: Rows of legionaries turning to salute Caesar, not the Senate standard

shots.narration: His wars made him enormously rich. And he spoke for ordinary Romans against the old elite. The people loved him.
shots.onScreen: Coins pour into a chest; crowd cheering in the Forum

shots.narration: Maybe they loved him too much.
shots.onScreen: The cheering crowd seen from a Senate window, a stern senator watching
shots.motion: slow push on the senator's frown

shots.narration: In 49 BC, the Senate and Caesar's great rival, Pompey, order him to give up his army and come home.
shots.onScreen: Map: letter icon flies from Rome to Caesar in Gaul
shots.overlay: callout: POMPEY THE GREAT / CAESAR'S RIVAL

shots.narration: Without his command, he would lose his legal protection. His enemies were waiting to put him on trial.
shots.onScreen: Courtroom with empty defendant's bench and waiting prosecutors
shots.motion: slow push on the empty bench

shots.narration: So Caesar does something no Roman general is allowed to do. He crosses the Rubicon river into Italy, with a legion behind him.
shots.onScreen: Map close on northern Italy; the Rubicon line; a legion icon steps across it

shots.narration: Roman law said generals had to leave their armies behind at that river. Crossing it with soldiers meant war.
shots.onScreen: Caesar on horseback in the shallow river, legion behind, mist

shots.narration: The civil war spreads across the whole Republic. In 48 BC, Caesar defeats Pompey in Greece. Pompey flees to Egypt and is killed there.
shots.onScreen: Map: battle icon at Pharsalus, Pompey's ship to Egypt, a dark X

shots.narration: The last of Pompey's armies is crushed in Spain in March 45 BC. Caesar has won.
shots.onScreen: Map: Munda in Spain flashes; the whole Republic turns Caesar red
shots.motion: crane back to show all of it

shots.narration: The Senate that once tried to stop him now gives him everything. Consul again and again. Then, in February 44 BC, dictator for life.
shots.onScreen: Senators raising hands; a scroll unrolls "DICTATOR PERPETUO"

shots.narration: Meanwhile, one word frightens Rome's old families more than any other. King.
shots.onScreen: A golden crown on a cushion, Senate hall in shadow behind

shots.narration: Rome had kings once. The last was Tarquin the Proud, a cruel tyrant.
shots.onScreen: Tarquin on a throne, stern brows, guards on either side
shots.overlay: callout: TARQUIN THE PROUD / LAST KING OF ROME

shots.narration: Around 509 BC, the Romans threw him out, and swore that no king would ever rule Rome again.
shots.onScreen: Crowd pushing Tarquin out of the city gate; senators raising hands in an oath

shots.narration: Now it looks as if Caesar wants to be one. He wears royal purple and puts up statues of himself around the city.
shots.onScreen: Caesar in a purple toga beside a new statue of himself

shots.narration: His allies rename the month of his birth, Quintilis, after him. Julius. We still call it July.
shots.onScreen: Calendar page flips from QUINTILIS to IULIUS to JULY

shots.narration: He even has a golden chair made for him in the Senate. The same chair he is sitting on today.
shots.onScreen: The golden chair gleams; the camera links it to Act 0's chair

shots.narration: For his enemies, Caesar is a threat to the Republic itself. They cannot beat him in battle. So they will have to find another way.
shots.onScreen: Shadowy figures in togas meeting by candlelight
shots.motion: slow push through the candle smoke

shots.narration: About sixty men join the plot. They come from very different places.
shots.onScreen: Sixty silhouettes in togas fill a dark hall

shots.narration: Some are old allies who feel Caesar never rewarded them enough.
shots.onScreen: Senator with an empty reward plate

shots.narration: Some fought against him for Pompey, and were pardoned by Caesar himself.
shots.onScreen: Former enemies receiving a pardon scroll from Caesar; red ink stamp "PARDONED"

shots.narration: A few simply believe in the Republic, and see a king coming.
shots.onScreen: A senator with a wax tablet reading "REPUBLIC"

shots.narration: And most belong to the old aristocracy, who run the Senate and do not want to share power with one man.
shots.onScreen: Rich senators at a banquet table, frowning at Caesar's statue

shots.narration: Their leaders include Marcus Brutus and Gaius Cassius.
shots.onScreen: Two figures step forward; name callouts
shots.overlay: callout: MARCUS BRUTUS · GAIUS CASSIUS / LEADING CONSPIRATORS

shots.narration: For months they meet in secret. And they look at different ways to do it.
shots.onScreen: A table with a city map and three wax tablets

shots.narration: Plan one. Attack him in the street, on the Via Sacra. Too public. His friends might be nearby.
shots.onScreen: Street scene on the Via Sacra, a red X stamps the tablet

shots.narration: Plan two. Throw him off a bridge, with armed men waiting below. Ambitious.
shots.onScreen: Tiny bridge model with tiny men underneath, a red X stamps it

shots.narration: Plan three. Hide among the gladiators at a show. Also rejected.
shots.onScreen: Arena model, red X stamps it

shots.narration: In the end they choose a meeting of the Senate on the fifteenth of March, the Ides.
shots.onScreen: Calendar with the 15th circled in red

shots.narration: Three days later, Caesar is leaving Rome on a huge new war in the east, against the Dacians and the Parthians.
shots.onScreen: Map: arrows from Rome toward Dacia and Parthia

shots.narration: Once he leaves, he will be out of reach for years, and he will come back with even more glory.
shots.onScreen: Caesar on horseback at the head of an army, sun behind

shots.narration: A Senate meeting is perfect. Weapons are not allowed inside, so no one will be armed. Except them.
shots.onScreen: Senate doorway with a sign of a crossed-out sword

shots.narration: Most senators are loyal to Caesar. But few will jump in front of a blade for him.
shots.onScreen: Rows of senators looking nervous, glancing at each other

shots.narration: On the morning of the fifteenth, daggers are carried into the Curia of Pompey.
shots.onScreen: Morning at the Curia, servants carry wooden boxes

shots.narration: They are hidden in the wooden boxes normally used to carry writing tablets.
shots.onScreen: Box lid opens a crack, a glint inside; lid closes

shots.narration: The conspirators take them out and hide them under their togas.
shots.onScreen: A senator adjusts his toga, a dagger shape vanishes beneath the fold

shots.narration: Outside, the gladiators take their places by the exits. If Caesar runs, he won't get far.
shots.onScreen: Gladiators spread to the courtyard exits, top-down plan view

shots.narration: The gladiators belong to Decimus Brutus, one of Caesar's closest friends. A man named in Caesar's own will.
shots.onScreen: Decimus Brutus with the will scroll; name callout

shots.narration: Caesar trusts him completely. He would never question why Decimus's gladiators are there.
shots.onScreen: Caesar and Decimus laughing together, Caesar's hand on his shoulder

shots.narration: And when Caesar arrives with Mark Antony, a senator named Gaius Trebonius takes Antony aside for a chat.
shots.onScreen: Trebonius steering Antony away from the door

shots.narration: Antony is big, strong, and completely loyal. The plotters made sure he would not be inside.
shots.onScreen: Antony's broad shoulders in frame as the doors close behind him
shots.motion: push in on the closing doors

shots.narration: They had thought about killing Antony too. They decided against it. Killing Caesar alone would look like punishing a tyrant, not a massacre.
shots.onScreen: Two scales: one figure vs two figures; the single figure stays

shots.narration: The stage is set. All they need now is a signal.
shots.onScreen: Wide shot of the hall, Caesar on his chair, sixty togas still

shots.narration: The signal is a senator called Tillius Cimber. He walks up to Caesar and begs him to bring his brother home from exile.
shots.onScreen: Cimber kneels before the chair, hands raised

shots.narration: Dozens of senators stand up and crowd around, all pleading for the same thing.
shots.onScreen: Togas rise from the benches and close in like a tide
shots.motion: top-down rotation as the ring tightens

shots.narration: Then Cimber grabs Caesar's toga and pulls it down off his shoulders.
shots.onScreen: Cimber grabs the toga; Caesar's surprised brows

shots.narration: Caesar shouts in shock. This is violence.
shots.onScreen: Caesar half-standing, mouth open

shots.narration: Behind him, a senator named Casca strikes first. The blow only grazes him.
shots.onScreen: Casca's silhouette behind the chair, a dark shape; cut to black on the strike

shots.narration: Caesar spins around and, according to one ancient writer, stabs Casca in the arm with his stylus. His pen. Sadly, the pen is not mightier than the sword.
shots.onScreen: Close on a writing stylus in Caesar's mitten hand; a tiny "OUCH" in comic font

shots.narration: In seconds, Caesar disappears inside a crowd of togas.
shots.onScreen: The ring of togas closes over the chair from above; no blades visible

shots.narration: Two of his loyal friends try to push through to him. They are pushed back.
shots.onScreen: Two senators shoved back at the edge of the crowd

shots.narration: Marcus Brutus is in the crowd too, and strikes as well.
shots.onScreen: Brutus's face among the togas, then cut to black

shots.narration: Caesar is struck twenty-three times. A doctor later said only one of those wounds was fatal, the second, to his chest.
shots.onScreen: Black screen with a white tally counting to 23; doctor's note card

shots.narration: And his famous last words? "Et tu, Brute," "you too, Brutus," comes from Shakespeare, written more than sixteen hundred years later.
shots.onScreen: Quill writing "ET TU, BRUTE?" on paper, a "SHAKESPEARE, 1599" stamp

shots.narration: One ancient writer says Caesar said nothing at all. Others say his last words were in Greek. "You too, child?"
shots.onScreen: Two cards: "SILENCE" and "KAI SU, TEKNON?"

shots.narration: He falls at the foot of a statue. A statue of Pompey, the rival he defeated, and refused to tear down.
shots.onScreen: The marble statue of Pompey looking down at the empty golden chair; a fallen toga at its base, no blood

shots.narration: Caesar should have seen it coming. Ancient writers say the warnings had been piling up for a month.
shots.onScreen: An hourglass turning back; sand flows upward

shots.narration: In February, a soothsayer named Spurinna made a sacrifice for him. The animal, it was said, had no heart.
shots.onScreen: An altar with smoke, Spurinna reading the omens; a red question mark

shots.narration: Spurinna warned him his life was in danger, and that it would come no later than the Ides of March.
shots.onScreen: Spurinna pointing at a calendar, 15 circled

shots.narration: On the night before, at dinner, the talk turned to the best kind of death. Caesar said, "A sudden one."
shots.onScreen: Dinner table, goblets, Caesar raising a hand

shots.narration: That night, the doors and windows of his bedroom flew open all at once.
shots.onScreen: Bedroom, shutters bang open, curtains blow in

shots.narration: His wife, Calpurnia, cried in her sleep. In the morning she begged him not to go. She had dreamed she was holding his body.
shots.onScreen: Calpurnia clutching Caesar's arm at dawn

shots.narration: Caesar was not very superstitious. But he called his own priests. Every sign they read was bad.
shots.onScreen: Priests shaking their heads over an altar

shots.narration: So he decided not to go.
shots.onScreen: Caesar sits back down, takes off his laurel

shots.narration: Then his friend Decimus Brutus came to the house. You called this meeting, he said. Will you really cancel it because of a dream?
shots.onScreen: Decimus at the doorway, persuasive hands

shots.narration: What would people say? That the dictator of Rome was afraid of his wife's dreams.
shots.onScreen: Imaginary gossip bubbles over Roman heads

shots.narration: So Caesar went.
shots.onScreen: Caesar puts the laurel back on and walks out

shots.narration: On the way, a teacher named Artemidorus pushed through the crowd and handed him a scroll. Read this now, he said. It is about you.
shots.onScreen: Artemidorus pressing a scroll into Caesar's hand in a busy street

shots.narration: It is said the scroll named the plot. Caesar never read it. He was still holding it when he walked into the Curia.
shots.onScreen: Scroll in Caesar's hand, unopened, as the Curia doors close

shots.narration: Meanwhile, the killers thought they had saved the Republic. Instead, they had made a hole in the middle of it.
shots.onScreen: Empty golden chair in a silent hall

shots.narration: Caesar's adopted son, Octavian, and his ally Mark Antony joined with the general Marcus Lepidus.
shots.onScreen: Three figures side by side; name callouts

shots.narration: Together they hunted the assassins down. In 42 BC, Brutus and Cassius were defeated at Philippi, in Greece.
shots.onScreen: Map: armies meet at Philippi

shots.narration: More war followed, until only one man was left. Octavian.
shots.onScreen: Last figure standing on a stage as others fade

shots.narration: In 27 BC, the Senate gave him a new name, Augustus. He became Rome's first emperor. The Republic was over.
shots.onScreen: Octavian crowned with laurel, title "AUGUSTUS"

shots.narration: Augustus did not make his father's mistakes.
shots.onScreen: Augustus looking at Caesar's statue

shots.narration: Caesar pardoned his enemies. He promoted them. He gave them honours. He even left Pompey's statues standing.
shots.onScreen: Caesar handing pardons to men who later appear in the plot; statue of Pompey

shots.narration: His mercy may be what killed him.
shots.onScreen: The statue of Pompey over the empty chair

shots.narration: Caesar was hated, but not feared. He showed his power openly, and made no effort to hide it.
shots.onScreen: Caesar in purple surrounded by statues of himself

shots.narration: The historian John Balsdon put it this way. The next ruler of Rome would have to wear a republican mask, however false.
shots.onScreen: A theatre mask of a Roman senator lowered over Augustus's face

shots.narration: Augustus wore that mask for forty years.
shots.onScreen: Augustus with the mask, crowds bowing

shots.narration: If you want more stories like this, subscribe. See you in the next one.
shots.onScreen: End card with subscribe button
